article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Indica-dominant hybrid
Genetics: Kashmir / North Indian × Nepalese Himalayan
Breeder: Barney’s Farm
THC Content: 22%
CBD Content: 1.2%
Terpene Profile: myrcene , pinene , caryophyllene
Primary Flavors: Sweet pine, earth, spice, mint, herbs
Flowering Time (Indoor): 60–65 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: Late September to early October
Indoor Yield: Up to 550 grams per square meter
Outdoor Yield: Potentially high
Grow Difficulty: Easy to moderate

Night Shade emerged from Barney’s Farm during a period when Himalayan cannabis genetics still held a prominent place in European breeding. Rather than leaning on the candy sweetness, Cookies ancestry, or extreme THC claims that define many newer cultivars, this older indica takes its character from mountain marijuana populations associated with Kashmir, northern India, and Nepal. The plant remains compact, forms unusually thick resinous flowers, and develops an aroma that moves between sweet pine, herbs, mint, incense, and earthy spice. Its effect is similarly traditional. The high may begin with a modest sense of warmth and contentment, but the experience increasingly settles into the body until relaxation becomes unmistakable. Night Shade earned additional recognition when Barney’s entered it in the 2006 High Times Cannabis Cup , where it finished third in the Indica category.
Genetics and Lineage

Historical Barney’s Farm descriptions identify Night Shade as a Himalayan hybrid built from Kashmir and Nepalese genetics. Some archived references describe the first side more broadly as North Indian, while others specifically use Kashmir. Those descriptions are compatible rather than necessarily contradictory: Kashmir lies within the western Himalayan region and has a long association with traditional cannabis and hashish-producing populations. For an authority strain reference, the safest pedigree is therefore Kashmir/North Indian × Nepalese rather than attempting to assign modern commercial strain names to either parent.

Both ancestral populations help explain the finished plant. Himalayan cannabis selected for resin production frequently develops compact floral structures, broad foliage, strong branching, and abundant trichomes. Generations of cultivation for hand-rubbed charas and other traditional preparations also placed considerable value on resin quality rather than simply flower size. Night Shade retains that old-world orientation, producing thick buds with a visibly sticky surface and an aroma much closer to pine, spice, herbs, and incense than contemporary fruit candy.

This is also what separates Barney’s Night Shade from the modern Connected Cannabis cultivar called Nightshade. Connected keeps its strain’s genetics proprietary, while Barney’s older variety has a documented Himalayan background. The two should be treated as completely separate cannabis cultivars despite the nearly identical names.
Effects and Experience

The onset tends to be less dramatic than the peak. Instead of an immediate cerebral rush, the experience can begin with a gradual warming sensation accompanied by an easier mood and reduced mental urgency. Thoughts may remain coherent, but there is usually little of the drive or rapid association associated with Haze -heavy weed. The strain encourages slowing down rather than looking for something new to do.

Physical relaxation becomes increasingly important after the initial phase. Arms and legs can begin to feel heavier, muscular tension fades into the background, and sitting or lying down becomes progressively more appealing. Historical descriptions portray the high as cozy, warm, and distinctly indica in character. That wording fits the experience well: the cultivar creates a feeling of physical enclosure rather than energetic expansion.

Dose can turn that relaxation into substantial sedation. At roughly 22% THC in historical breeder material, Night Shade was potent by the standards of its era and remains strong enough to command respect today. Larger servings are much better suited to late evenings than productive daytime activity. Dry mouth, dry eyes, dizziness, short-term memory impairment, and excessive sleepiness are possible when intake exceeds personal tolerance.
Medical Benefits

Night Shade has traditionally appealed to medical marijuana consumers who prefer a body-centered cannabis experience. Deep physical relaxation may temporarily make muscle tightness or general discomfort less intrusive, while the calmer mental state can be attractive when stress interferes with unwinding. The gradual development of sleepiness also helps explain why the strain has long been associated with nighttime use.

Historical descriptions additionally connected the cultivar with appetite, discomfort, and sleep-related concerns. These potential uses should be interpreted carefully. A named weed strain is not a standardized medicine, and Night Shade itself has not been validated in controlled clinical trials as a treatment for insomnia, chronic pain, anxiety, chemotherapy side effects, or other specific conditions.

The approximately 1.2% CBD figure reported for the historical strain is higher than the trace levels found in many modern THC-dominant cultivars, although it remains far below the concentrations associated with CBD-rich marijuana. Anyone using cannabis for a medical purpose should rely on laboratory results from the actual flower being consumed and discuss high-THC products with a qualified healthcare professional when medications or significant health conditions are involved.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Sweet pine is the defining aromatic feature in preserved breeder descriptions. Opening a well-cured flower can produce a fresh evergreen quality accompanied by damp earth, herbs, and dry spice. With more handling, sharper notes emerge. Mint, pepper, incense, and a slightly resinous hash-like scent can sit beneath the sweeter pine, giving the aroma considerably more complexity than a simple “Kush” profile.

The flavor follows a similarly traditional path. Pine and mild sweetness generally lead the inhale, followed by earthy herbs and spice through the middle. Some expressions develop an almost mint-like freshness, while the finish can resemble incense or traditional resin. A contemporary review from Barney’s Amsterdam shortly after the cultivar’s Cannabis Cup appearance also noted an unusual peppery, green-herbal quality in the flower.

No original Barney’s Farm terpene laboratory panel appears to have survived with the cultivar, so exact terpene percentages should not be presented as established genetics. Modern references often associate it with compounds such as myrcene, pinene, caryophyllene, linalool, and limonene, but environmental conditions, phenotype, harvest maturity, drying, and storage can significantly change the aromatic chemistry of any cannabis crop.
Growing Information

Compact growth was one of Night Shade’s defining horticultural traits. Historical descriptions place indoor height at only about 50–60 centimeters, considerably shorter than many hybrid marijuana plants. The structure remains bushy rather than lanky, and mature branches develop unusually large, dense flowers with prominent trichome coverage. That combination makes the plant naturally compatible with indoor spaces where vertical clearance is limited.

Flowering normally requires approximately 60–65 days, placing the cultivar in the eight-to-nine-week range. Under favorable indoor conditions, historical Barney’s specifications put production at about 550 grams per square meter. The flowers can become extremely thick relative to the plant’s modest stature, so maintaining airflow through the canopy becomes increasingly important late in bloom. Persistent humidity around dense buds can create conditions favorable to mold.

Outdoor maturity typically arrives from late September into early October. The relatively fast finish reflects the seasonal adaptation expected from Himalayan genetics and gives the cultivar an advantage in places where autumn weather deteriorates quickly. Despite its exotic geographical ancestry, Night Shade was remembered as a relatively uncomplicated plant to cultivate, combining manageable height, fast flowering, and substantial flower formation.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Barney’s Farm Night Shade?

Night Shade was bred from Himalayan cannabis genetics associated with Kashmir or northern India and Nepal. Historical Barney’s descriptions commonly list the parents as Kashmir × Nepalese. It should not be confused with Connected Cannabis Co.’s modern Nightshade strain, whose genetics are proprietary.
Is Night Shade indica or sativa?
Night Shade is strongly indica-dominant. Its short, bushy structure, dense flowers, fast flowering period, and progressively heavy physical effect all support that classification.
How strong is Night Shade weed?

Historical Barney’s Farm material lists THC at approximately 22% and CBD around 1.2%. That made it a particularly potent indica when it was released. Actual cannabinoid levels can vary depending on phenotype and cultivation, so modern flower should be judged by its own laboratory analysis.
What does Night Shade taste like?

Sweet pine is the signature flavor, accompanied by earth, herbs, mint, spice, pepper, and incense. The profile is much closer to classic Himalayan or old-school indica cannabis than modern candy and dessert strains .
How long does Night Shade take to flower?

Indoor flowering generally requires about 60–65 days, or roughly eight to nine weeks. Historical breeder material lists indoor plants around 50–60 centimeters tall with yields reaching approximately 550 grams per square meter. Outdoors, harvest usually falls around late September or early October.
Final Thoughts on Night Shade

Night Shade belongs to an era of European marijuana breeding when Himalayan genetics were valued for much more than their historical reputation. Barney’s Farm used Kashmir/North Indian and Nepalese material to create a cultivar with tangible practical advantages: compact growth, fast maturation, heavy resin production, dense flowers, and a powerful indica-oriented experience. Its third-place finish in the Indica category at the 2006 High Times Cannabis Cup added international recognition to a strain already built around traditional cannabis traits.

The flavor is equally rooted in that older lineage. Sweet pine, mint, herbs, earth, pepper, and incense create a profile far removed from the syrupy fruit and dessert aromas common today. Combined with the creeping transition from gentle euphoria into substantial body relaxation, those qualities give Barney’s Night Shade a clear identity. For cannabis enthusiasts researching classic European marijuana strains or Himalayan-derived weed, it remains an interesting example of Barney’s Farm’s earlier work with traditional indica genetics.
